# Goal
I've made a boxplot of dog weights. I then plotted a histogram of the weights of pitbulls as well as a histogram of the z scores.  
```{r}
#myDogAnalysis.R

#read in the dog weight file

dog_weights <- read.csv("data/dog_weights.csv")

#make a boxplot separating values by breed
boxplot(dog_weights$dog_weight ~ dog_weights$dog_type, 
        col = c("red", "green", "pink"), 
        main = "Dog Weights (lbs)",
        ylab = "Weight (lbs)",
        xlab = "Dog Breed",
        cex.lab = 1,
        cex.main = 1
        )

#Make two histograms of the raw data and zscores of pitbull weights
library(dplyr)
par(mfrow=c(1,2))
pitbull <- filter(dog_weights, dog_type=="pitbull") 
zscore <- scale(pitbull$dog_weight)
hist((pitbull$dog_weight), 
     main="Raw Pitbull Weights", 
     xlab="weight",
      col=c("orange"))
hist(zscore, 
     main="Pitbull Weight Z-Scores",
     xlab="Z-Score",
     col=c("blue")
     )
#I am now running a one sample t-test to test whether the weight of beagles  is significantly different from 21 pounds
beagle <- filter(dog_weights, dog_type == "beagle")
t.test(beagle$dog_weight, mu = 21)

#I am now performing a two sample t-test to test whether the weight of pitbulls  is significantly different from the weight of dalmations
dalmatian <- filter(dog_weights, dog_type == "dalmatian")
t.test(pitbull$dog_weight, dalmatian$dog_weight)



```
# Intepretation
I'd say these results are quite wonderfully superb! The mean weight of beagles (19.9118 lbs) was not significantly different from 21 pounds (p = 0.09453). However, pitbulls and dalmatians differed significantly in weight (p < .001), with dalmatians weighing more on average than pitbulls.
